_readme: Per-repo translation POLICY for the shared i18n guards, read by
check-locale-coverage.ts and by both ingestion scripts via --policy.
Committed rather than passed on the command line: restating a rule
per run is how it becomes a reflex, and a flag people always pass
guards nothing.
requiredLiterals — strings the app compares TYPED USER INPUT against.
A locale that translates one renders a gate no speaker of that
language can pass. Enforced at ingestion because surfaces at risk
include apps with no coverage guard of their own (apps/defi's
recovery page compares against the same word).
omissions / empty — the narrow linguistic exemptions, bound to the
exact locale:key(:token) so each excuses itself and nothing else.
acceptedAsTranslated — leaves whose value is CORRECT even though it
matches the English word for word, so the match is not evidence of a
gap. Each entry carries a written reason AND the English value it
was granted against: if en.json moves on, the exemption goes stale
and is reported rather than silently inherited. Most entries are
identical to the English; where a locale is instead built from the
same words in a different order (French 'Mode strict' for 'Strict
mode'), record that exact value under 'values' so rewording it
retires the exemption instead of leaving it armed.
The same scope also excuses a fragment that correctly holds no words
at all because a sister fragment carries them (see footerParts.tail).
There are deliberately NO pattern-based exemptions. Punctuation is
localized (consentParts.suffix is '.' in English and '。' in
Chinese), so a no-letters rule would have let a real localization
regress unnoticed. Everything else identical to English belongs in
english-valued-baseline.json, which is meant to shrink.

ar:copy.units.durationDay_two.reason: Arabic dual encodes the count in the noun (يومان = 'two days'); restating {{count}} renders '2 يومان'

ar:copy.units.durationMonth_two.reason: Arabic dual encodes the count in the noun

ar:copy.units.durationYear_two.reason: Arabic dual encodes the count in the noun

empty.ja:copy.consentParts.prefix: Japanese puts the verb last; the suffix carries the agreement the English states up front

copy.app.name.reason: The product name. A brand is not translated.

copy.claims.row.amountWithSuffix.reason: Two interpolated values and nothing else — there are no words in this string.

copy.desk.signed.rateLine.reason: Two interpolated values around APR, itself a standard finance acronym; there is no prose here to translate.

copy.desk.statUnknown.reason: The em dash marking an unavailable value on the trading desk (DeskHeader, OrderTicket). It is a symbol, not a word, and all nine locales render it identically on purpose — recorded here rather than in the baseline because it is not debt anyone can pay: the only way it could ever leave a shrink-only backlog is by being replaced with a different glyph, which would be a regression rather than a translation.

copy.desk.ticket.expiryGtc.reason: GTC — standard order-duration acronym, used untranslated on trading surfaces in every locale.

copy.desk.ticket.fillAon.reason: AON — standard fill-type acronym, used untranslated on trading surfaces in every locale.

copy.desk.ticket.fillIoc.reason: IOC — standard fill-type acronym, used untranslated on trading surfaces in every locale.

copy.offers.footerParts.tail.reason: The closing fragment of a sentence split around two inline links. English trails the sentence with the noun (' flows.'); German, Spanish and French put that noun in the LEAD fragment instead ('… wie die gefuehrten Ablaeufe ', '… los flujos guiados de ', '… les parcours guides '), so the tail is correctly nothing but the full stop. The words are present in the rendered sentence, just in a different fragment — which is what splitting a sentence into parts costs, and a per-fragment check cannot see.

copy.riskAccess.strict.title.reason: French 'Mode strict' is the correct rendering of 'Strict mode' — the noun-adjective order is French grammar, and both words are French. The word comparison is a multiset, so it cannot tell this from a rearranged English sentence; the accepted French is recorded below so rewording it retires this entry.
